paragraphs.heading: What conductivity measures
paragraphs.text: Electrical conductivity describes how well a material lets electric current pass through it. Its partner, resistivity, describes how strongly a material pushes back against that current. The two are reciprocals, so if you know one you can work out the other. Both belong to the material itself rather than to any particular object made from it.

paragraphs.heading: Symbols and units
paragraphs.text: Resistivity is usually written with the Greek letter ρ (rho) and measured in ohm-metres (Ω⋅m). Conductivity is usually written σ (sigma), though κ (kappa) and γ (gamma) are sometimes used instead, κ especially in electrical engineering. Its SI unit is the siemens per metre (S/m). A low resistivity, and so a high conductivity, marks a material that carries current readily.

paragraphs.heading: Material versus object
paragraphs.text: Resistivity and conductivity describe a material, while resistance and conductance describe one specific object. Resistivity can be pictured as the opposition of a standard cube of the material to current. A real object's resistance also depends on its shape: it rises with length and falls as the cross-sectional area grows. So every pure copper wire has the same resistivity, yet a long, thin copper wire has far more resistance than a short, thick one.

paragraphs.heading: A water pipe picture
paragraphs.text: Current flowing through a material can be compared with water pushed through a pipe. A high-resistivity material is like a pipe packed with sand, and a low-resistivity one is like an empty pipe. If the two pipes have the same size and shape, the sandy one resists the flow more. But length and width matter too: short or wide pipes let water through more easily than long or narrow ones.

paragraphs.heading: Copper and rubber
paragraphs.text: Every material has its own resistivity, and materials differ enormously. Rubber has a large ρ and a small σ: even a very strong electric field drives almost no current through it. Copper is the opposite, with a small ρ and a large σ, so even a weak field pulls a lot of current along.

paragraphs.heading: Where current comes from
paragraphs.text: Electric current is the orderly movement of charged particles. The equation J⃗ = qnv⃗_d links the current density J⃗ to the charge of each carrier, how many carriers there are, and their drift velocity, which is their averaged long-term motion. Quantum mechanics says that an electron inside an atom or a crystal is limited to certain exact energies. When many allowed levels lie very close together, they are grouped into an energy band, and a material can have many such bands.
